title: Motor Systems: Upper vs Lower Motor Neurons
summary: How movement is commanded and how to tell where the motor system is broken.

lessons.title: The Motor Hierarchy

levels.kid:
Moving your body is like a big team with a boss, managers and workers.

The boss is the top of your brain. It decides, "I want to grab that cookie!"

The message zooms down long wires through your brain and into your spinal cord. In the spinal cord, worker nerve cells get the message and tell your muscles to squeeze.

Two helper coaches watch and fix things. One makes your moves smooth and on target. The other helps start the right moves and stop the wrong ones.

And guess what? The wires cross over, so the left side of your brain moves your right hand!
levels.hs:
Movement is organized in **levels**, like a company.

- **Planning (top)**: frontal areas in front of the motor cortex, the **premotor cortex** and **supplementary motor area**, plan and sequence movements. The parietal lobe tells them where things are in space.
- **Command**: the **primary motor cortex** in the **precentral gyrus** sends the go signal. It has a body map (motor homunculus) with huge areas for the hands and mouth.
- **Brainstem**: relays and posture pathways that keep you balanced and upright.
- **Spinal cord**: **motor neurons** in the ventral (front) horn send axons out to muscles. The cord also has built-in circuits for reflexes and rhythms like walking.

The main highway is the **corticospinal tract**: from the cortex, through the internal capsule and brainstem, to the **pyramids** of the medulla, where most fibers **cross** to the other side. So the left brain controls the right body.

Two "side loops" adjust movement without sending commands straight to muscles:
- **Cerebellum**: coordination, timing, accuracy
- **Basal ganglia**: choosing and starting the right movement, suppressing unwanted ones (problems cause Parkinson disease)

Doctors call neurons from the brain to the cord **upper motor neurons** and those from the cord to muscle **lower motor neurons**.
levels.college:
**Levels of the motor hierarchy:**
- **Association cortex** (posterior parietal, prefrontal): goals and spatial targets.
- **Premotor cortex** (lateral area 6): movements guided by external cues; **supplementary motor area** (medial area 6): internally generated and sequenced movements, bimanual coordination. Both project to M1 and directly to the cord.
- **Primary motor cortex (M1, area 4)**: encodes force and direction; somatotopic, with the leg on the medial surface (ACA territory) and the hand and face laterally (MCA territory).
- **Brainstem** descending systems.
- **Spinal cord**: alpha and gamma motor neurons, interneurons, and central pattern generators for locomotion.

**Corticospinal tract route**: corona radiata → **posterior limb of internal capsule** → middle of the **cerebral peduncle** → basis pontis → **medullary pyramids** → about 85–90% decussate at the **pyramidal decussation** to form the **lateral corticospinal tract** (distal limb muscles); the uncrossed remainder forms the **anterior corticospinal tract** (axial muscles). Only about a third of fibers arise from M1; the rest come from premotor, SMA and parietal cortex.

**Corticobulbar fibers** supply cranial nerve motor nuclei, mostly bilaterally. Exception: the lower face receives mainly contralateral input, so a cortical lesion weakens the lower face but spares the forehead.

**Medial vs lateral systems (Kuypers)**:
- Medial: reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, tectospinal, anterior corticospinal → axial and proximal muscles, posture, orienting.
- Lateral: lateral corticospinal and rubrospinal → distal limb, fine and fractionated movement.
In the ventral horn, medial motor neurons supply axial muscles; lateral ones supply distal muscles.

**Side loops**: cerebellum and basal ganglia project through the thalamus (VL/VA) back to cortex. They alter motor output without direct projections to motor neurons.

**Posturing**: decorticate (arm flexion, leg extension) suggests a lesion above the red nucleus; decerebrate (extension of all limbs) suggests brainstem damage below it, both ominous in coma.
levels.phd:
**What does M1 encode?** Georgopoulos showed that M1 neurons are broadly tuned to movement direction and that a population vector predicts reach direction, while Evarts linked M1 firing to force. A dynamical systems view (Churchland, Shenoy) treats M1 population activity as a rotational dynamical system: preparatory activity sets an initial state from which movement-generating dynamics unfold, rather than each neuron representing a parameter. This framing explains why preparatory activity does not cause movement: it lies in an "output-null" subspace.

**Corticomotoneuronal connections.** In primates, a subset of corticospinal neurons from caudal M1 ("new M1") synapses monosynaptically on spinal motor neurons, especially those for hand muscles (Lemon, Rathelot and Strick). These direct connections scale with manual dexterity across species and underlie independent finger movement. Rodents largely lack them, a key caveat when translating motor recovery studies.

**Reticulospinal contribution.** Once thought to control only posture, the reticulospinal system contributes to reaching and even hand function in primates (Baker). After corticospinal damage, reticulospinal upregulation may support gross recovery, at the cost of mass synergies (shoulder abduction coupled with elbow flexion) and possibly spasticity.

**Spinal circuitry.** Central pattern generators produce rhythmic flexor-extensor alternation without supraspinal input, demonstrated in spinal cats on treadmills. Genetically defined interneuron classes (V0, V1, V2a, V3, dI6) set left-right alternation and rhythm. Epidural electrical stimulation in humans with chronic spinal cord injury can engage these circuits, allowing stepping when combined with rehabilitation, which is reshaping the view that complete paralysis is permanent.

**Hierarchy vs heterarchy.** The strict top-down metaphor is misleading: premotor, SMA and cingulate motor areas project directly to the cord in parallel with M1, and feedback loops through cerebellum and basal ganglia operate continuously. Optimal feedback control models describe movement as continuous correction rather than pre-planned command execution.
levels.expert:
**Why the hierarchy matters in the OR.** Neurosurgeons operate near motor cortex and its tracts routinely, so knowing where movement lives is the difference between a good resection and a hemiplegic patient.

**Localization tools:**
- **Anatomy**: the precentral gyrus is identified on MRI by the hand knob (an inverted omega shape) and the "pars marginalis" sign; the central sulcus usually runs continuous to the medial surface.
- **fMRI and navigated TMS** map motor cortex before surgery.
- **DTI tractography** reconstructs the corticospinal tract to show its relation to a tumor.
- **Intraoperative direct cortical stimulation** (Penfield's method): stimulating the cortex evokes movement, confirming motor areas. Subcortical stimulation estimates the distance to the corticospinal tract during resection.
- **Motor evoked potentials** monitor the tract continuously; a significant drop prompts the surgeon to stop, irrigate warm saline, raise blood pressure or reposition retractors.

**SMA syndrome**: after resecting the supplementary motor area, patients can have contralateral akinesia and, on the dominant side, speech arrest that **largely recovers over weeks**. Recognizing it prevents panic and unnecessary reoperation, and preoperative counseling is essential. This is a classic difference between SMA and M1/corticospinal injury, which causes lasting deficit.

**Localization from the bedside:**
- Face, arm more than leg weakness: lateral convexity (MCA) or upper corona radiata.
- Leg more than arm: medial frontal (ACA) or parasagittal mass (e.g., falcine meningioma) or spinal cord.
- Face, arm and leg equally: internal capsule or pons (pure motor lacunar stroke).
- Crossed signs (cranial nerve on one side, limbs on the other): brainstem.

**Posturing in trauma**: decorticate and decerebrate posturing score low on the GCS motor scale (3 and 2). Decerebrate posturing after head injury suggests brainstem compression and needs urgent imaging and often decompression.

**Pitfall**: a lesion in the parasagittal region can cause bilateral leg weakness and urinary symptoms, mimicking spinal cord disease. If the spine MRI is normal, image the head.

keyPoints: Planning: premotor cortex and SMA (area 6); command: primary motor cortex (area 4, precentral gyrus)
Corticospinal tract: internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pyramids; 85–90% cross to form the lateral corticospinal tract
Medial systems (reticulo-, vestibulo-, tectospinal) control posture; lateral systems control distal limbs
Cerebellum and basal ganglia are side loops acting via the thalamus, not directly on motor neurons
Lower face gets mainly contralateral cortical input; forehead is bilateral
Decorticate posturing = lesion above red nucleus; decerebrate = below

lessons.title: Motor Units & the Neuromuscular Junction

levels.kid:
Each muscle is made of lots of tiny threads called muscle fibers. One nerve cell controls a little team of these fibers. The nerve cell plus its team is called a motor unit.

To pick up a feather, your body uses just a few small teams. To lift a heavy backpack, it calls in lots of big teams!

Where the nerve touches the muscle, there is a tiny gap. The nerve sends a chemical messenger across the gap, like tossing a ball. When the muscle catches it, the muscle squeezes.

Some sicknesses stop the ball from being caught, and then muscles get weak and tired.
levels.hs:
A **motor unit** is one **alpha motor neuron** plus all the muscle fibers it controls. When that neuron fires, all its fibers contract together.

Motor units vary in size. Eye muscles have tiny motor units (few fibers each) for precise control. Big leg muscles have huge motor units with many hundreds of fibers for power.

Your body controls force in two ways:
- **Recruitment**: adding more motor units, small ones first, big ones later (the **size principle**)
- **Rate coding**: making each unit fire faster

The **neuromuscular junction (NMJ)** is the synapse between nerve and muscle:
1. An action potential reaches the nerve terminal.
2. **Calcium** rushes in through voltage-gated channels.
3. Vesicles release **acetylcholine (ACh)**.
4. ACh binds **nicotinic receptors** on the muscle, opening channels and depolarizing the muscle.
5. The muscle fires an action potential and contracts.
6. **Acetylcholinesterase** breaks down ACh to end the signal.

Diseases of the NMJ:
- **Myasthenia gravis**: antibodies attack ACh receptors, causing weakness that gets worse with use, droopy eyelids and double vision.
- **Botulism**: a bacterial toxin blocks ACh release, causing paralysis.
- **Nerve agents and some insecticides** block acetylcholinesterase, flooding synapses with ACh.
levels.college:
**Motor units and recruitment.** Innervation ratios range from a handful of fibers per neuron in extraocular muscles to well over a thousand in leg muscles like gastrocnemius. Motor unit types:
- **S (slow, type I fibers)**: small neurons, low force, fatigue-resistant, oxidative.
- **FR (fast fatigue-resistant, type IIa)**.
- **FF (fast fatigable, type IIx)**: large neurons, high force.
**Henneman's size principle**: smaller motor neurons have higher input resistance and reach threshold first, so recruitment proceeds S → FR → FF automatically. Force is graded by recruitment and rate coding (summation toward tetanus).

**NMJ transmission:**
- Presynaptic depolarization opens **P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels**.
- Calcium triggers vesicle fusion via **SNARE proteins** (synaptobrevin on vesicles; syntaxin and SNAP-25 on the membrane) and the sensor synaptotagmin.
- ACh binds the **muscle nicotinic receptor** (adult form two alpha, beta, delta, epsilon subunits), a nonselective cation channel, producing the **end-plate potential**.
- The end-plate potential normally far exceeds threshold: the **safety factor**.
- Muscle action potentials spread along T-tubules; the DHPR voltage sensor couples to RyR1 to release calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
- Acetylcholinesterase in the synaptic cleft hydrolyzes ACh.

**Disorders by site:**
- **Myasthenia gravis** (postsynaptic): antibodies to AChR (or MuSK, LRP4) reduce functional receptors and the safety factor. Fatigable ptosis, diplopia, bulbar and proximal weakness. **Decrement** on slow repetitive nerve stimulation.
- **Lambert-Eaton syndrome** (presynaptic): antibodies to P/Q calcium channels, often paraneoplastic with small cell lung cancer. Proximal weakness, autonomic symptoms, reduced reflexes; strength and reflexes briefly **improve after exercise**; **increment** with high-frequency stimulation.
- **Botulism**: toxin light chains cleave SNAREs (type A cleaves SNAP-25), blocking release; descending paralysis with dilated pupils.
- **Organophosphates**: acetylcholinesterase inhibition → cholinergic crisis; treated with atropine and pralidoxime.

**Pharmacology**: succinylcholine is a depolarizing blocker; rocuronium is a nondepolarizing competitive antagonist, reversed by sugammadex (encapsulation) or neostigmine (cholinesterase inhibition).
levels.phd:
**Safety factor architecture.** NMJ reliability rests on postsynaptic folds dense with AChR at their crests and voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.4) in their troughs, which lower the local threshold. Quantal content (vesicles released per impulse) is high, and receptor density near saturating. Myasthenia erodes this margin: complement-mediated (membrane attack complex) destruction flattens folds and removes receptors, so the end-plate potential falls closer to threshold and some fibers fail, especially during repetitive firing as vesicle availability declines. This explains the decrement on repetitive stimulation and the increased jitter and blocking on single-fiber EMG, the most sensitive test.

**Agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling.** Motor neuron-derived agrin binds LRP4, activating the receptor tyrosine kinase MuSK, which with rapsyn clusters AChR. MuSK antibodies (IgG4, non-complement-fixing) disrupt this signaling rather than destroying receptors, producing a distinct phenotype: bulbar and neck predominance, poor response to cholinesterase inhibitors, and excellent response to B-cell depletion (rituximab). This illustrates how antibody subclass shapes mechanism and therapy.

**Therapeutic logic in myasthenia.** Because AChR-antibody disease is complement-dependent and IgG1/IgG3-mediated, terminal complement inhibitors (eculizumab, ravulizumab, zilucoplan) and neonatal Fc receptor blockers (efgartigimod, rozanolixizumab), which accelerate IgG catabolism, are effective. Thymectomy benefits AChR-positive generalized disease (MGTX trial), reflecting the thymus as a site of autoimmune priming; thymoma occurs in a subset.

**Motor unit physiology.** Size principle recruitment arises from intrinsic properties plus persistent inward currents (PICs) mediated by dendritic calcium and sodium channels, amplified by serotonin and norepinephrine from the brainstem. PICs allow self-sustained firing and are a target of interest in spasticity. High-density surface EMG decomposition now resolves individual motor unit discharges noninvasively, enabling studies of common synaptic drive and neural interfaces.

**Development and plasticity**: the fetal gamma subunit is replaced by epsilon after birth; denervation re-expresses gamma-containing receptors spread across the fiber, causing supersensitivity and fibrillation potentials.
levels.expert:
**Recognizing NMJ disease.** The key word is **fatigability**: weakness that worsens with sustained or repeated use and improves with rest. Look for:
- Ptosis worsening on sustained upgaze, and diplopia that varies; pupils are always normal in myasthenia.
- Bulbar fatigue: nasal speech while counting aloud, choking, jaw tiring while chewing.
- Proximal and neck flexor weakness.
- **Ice pack test**: cooling improves ptosis by slowing acetylcholinesterase.

**Workup**: AChR antibodies, then MuSK and LRP4 if negative; repetitive nerve stimulation; single-fiber EMG (most sensitive); **chest CT for thymoma** in every new myasthenia patient. Thymoma is a surgical tumor; complete resection is the goal.

**Myasthenic crisis** is respiratory failure from weakness: monitor **forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force** rather than oxygen saturation, which falls late. Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange and intubate early when vital capacity falls. Avoid drugs that worsen myasthenia, including aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, some beta-blockers, and use neuromuscular blockers cautiously (patients are very sensitive to nondepolarizing agents and resistant to succinylcholine).

**Lambert-Eaton**: proximal leg weakness, dry mouth, constipation, reduced reflexes that return after brief maximal contraction. Search hard for **small cell lung cancer**, sometimes repeatedly over years. Amifampridine (potassium channel blocker that prolongs depolarization) helps.

**Botulism**: descending symmetric paralysis starting with cranial nerves (diplopia, dysphagia), dilated unreactive pupils, no sensory loss, alert patient. Sources include foodborne, wound (contaminated injection sites) and infant forms. Give antitoxin early on clinical suspicion; don't wait for confirmation.

**Organophosphate poisoning**: muscarinic excess (salivation, bronchorrhea, bradycardia, miosis) plus nicotinic weakness and fasciculations. Atropine treats muscarinic effects; pralidoxime reactivates the enzyme before "aging".

**Neurosurgical anesthesia note**: neuromuscular blockade abolishes motor evoked potentials, so anesthesia teams avoid or carefully titrate paralytics during motor monitoring.

keyPoints: Motor unit = one alpha motor neuron + all the muscle fibers it innervates
Size principle: small, fatigue-resistant units are recruited first; force also rises by rate coding
NMJ: Ca2+ entry → SNARE-mediated ACh release → nicotinic AChR → end-plate potential; AChE ends it
Myasthenia gravis: anti-AChR (postsynaptic), fatigable weakness, decrement on slow repetitive stimulation
Lambert-Eaton: anti-P/Q Ca2+ channel (presynaptic), small cell lung cancer, improves after exercise
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNAREs; organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase (treat with atropine + pralidoxime)

lessons.title: Upper Motor Neuron Signs

levels.kid:
Remember the boss nerve cells at the top of the brain? Doctors call them upper motor neurons. Their long wires carry move messages down to the spinal cord.

If the boss wires get hurt, like in a stroke, the muscles still work but they don't get good orders.

The muscles get weak. They also get stiff and tight, like a rubber band pulled too hard. When the doctor taps the knee with a little hammer, the leg kicks extra big!

And when the doctor scratches the bottom of the foot, the big toe goes UP instead of curling down. That is a clue the boss wires are hurt.
levels.hs:
**Upper motor neurons (UMNs)** start in the motor cortex or brainstem and send axons down to the spinal cord or cranial nerve nuclei. The corticospinal tract is the main UMN pathway. They do not touch muscles directly; they control **lower motor neurons**.

When UMNs are damaged, doctors see:
- **Weakness**, often in a typical pattern: arm extensors and leg flexors weakest
- **Spasticity**: stiffness that is worse when you move the limb faster
- **Hyperreflexia**: overly brisk reflexes
- **Clonus**: rhythmic beating of a joint, like the ankle, after a quick stretch
- **Babinski sign**: big toe goes up when the sole is stroked
- **Little muscle wasting** (only from disuse) and **no fasciculations**

Why stiffness and brisk reflexes? The brain normally calms spinal reflex circuits. Lose that calming input and the reflexes become overactive.

Right after a sudden injury (a big stroke or spinal cord injury), muscles may first be **floppy** with absent reflexes (**shock**). Spasticity develops over days to weeks.

Causes include stroke, multiple sclerosis, brain or spinal tumors, spinal cord compression, and ALS (which damages both upper and lower motor neurons).
levels.college:
**Definition**: UMNs are neurons whose axons descend from cortex or brainstem to influence LMNs, mainly the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, plus reticulospinal and other descending systems.

**UMN syndrome**:
- **Negative features**: weakness in a **pyramidal distribution** (upper limb extensors and abductors weaker than flexors; lower limb flexors and dorsiflexors weaker than extensors), loss of dexterity and fine finger movement, slowed rapid alternating movements, **pronator drift**.
- **Positive features**: spasticity (velocity-dependent increase in tone, often clasp-knife), hyperreflexia with spread to adjacent muscles, clonus, **Babinski** and **Hoffmann** signs, flexor or extensor spasms.
- **Lost superficial reflexes**: abdominal and cremasteric reflexes.
- No fasciculations; atrophy mild and late (disuse).

**Acute shock phase**: cerebral or spinal shock causes initial flaccidity and areflexia, evolving to spasticity over days to weeks.

**Localizing a UMN lesion**:
- **Cortex**: contralateral, often with cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, field cuts, seizures); face-arm (MCA) or leg (ACA) predominant.
- **Internal capsule**: contralateral face, arm and leg equally (pure motor lacunar stroke).
- **Brainstem**: crossed findings, e.g., **Weber syndrome** (midbrain): ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis.
- **Spinal cord**: bilateral or ipsilateral signs below the lesion, a sensory level, bladder involvement, face spared.

**Central vs peripheral facial weakness**: a UMN lesion weakens the contralateral lower face and spares the forehead; an LMN (facial nerve) lesion weakens the whole ipsilateral face.

**Causes**: stroke, MS, tumor, trauma, cervical spondylotic myelopathy, B12 deficiency, hereditary spastic paraplegia, primary lateral sclerosis, ALS (with LMN signs).
levels.phd:
**The "pyramidal" misnomer.** Pure lesions of the medullary pyramid in primates (Tower; Lawrence and Kuypers) cause loss of fine finger movements and hypotonia rather than prominent spasticity. Spasticity and hyperreflexia arise mainly when **parapyramidal** fibers, cortico-reticular projections and descending reticulospinal and vestibulospinal systems are involved, as occurs in nearly all human capsular, brainstem and spinal lesions. The dorsal reticulospinal tract normally inhibits spinal reflexes; loss of its cortical drive, with relatively preserved excitatory medial reticulospinal and vestibulospinal output, tips the balance toward hyperexcitability.

**Mechanisms of spasticity.** Spasticity is not mainly gamma motor neuron overactivity, as once taught; microneurography shows little increase in spindle sensitivity. Instead:
- Reduced presynaptic inhibition of Ia afferent terminals
- Reduced reciprocal Ia inhibition and recurrent (Renshaw) inhibition
- Reduced post-activation depression at the Ia-motor neuron synapse
- Increased motor neuron excitability through **persistent inward currents**, re-emerging after injury through serotonin receptor constitutive activity (5-HT2C) in the cord
- Changes in muscle and connective tissue (stiffness, contracture) adding non-neural resistance

**Babinski sign physiology.** The extensor plantar response is part of the flexion withdrawal synergy, in which extensor hallucis longus behaves as a flexor (shortener) of the limb. Normally corticospinal input suppresses toe extension in this reflex; corticospinal dysfunction releases it. Its presence in infants reflects immature corticospinal myelination.

**Motor recovery.** After stroke, recovery follows a stereotyped course (Twitchell, Brunnstrom): flaccidity, then synergies with spasticity, then gradual isolated movement. The proportional recovery rule suggests many patients regain about 70% of their maximal possible improvement within months, but those with severely damaged corticospinal tracts (absent MEPs) are "non-fitters", making corticospinal integrity measured by TMS or DTI a key prognostic biomarker.
levels.expert:
**Examining for UMN signs efficiently:**
- **Pronator drift**: arms out, palms up, eyes closed. The weak arm pronates and drifts down, often the first sign of a subtle corticospinal lesion.
- **Finger tapping and fine finger movements**: slowed and clumsy early.
- **Tone**: rapid passive flexion and extension of elbow and knee; supinate the forearm quickly to catch spasticity.
- **Reflexes**: compare sides; look for spread (tapping the biceps produces finger flexion) and crossed adductor responses.
- **Hoffmann sign, Babinski, ankle clonus**.

**Cervical spondylotic myelopathy** is the most common cause of spinal cord dysfunction in older adults and a core neurosurgical diagnosis:
- Clumsy hands, trouble with buttons and handwriting, gait imbalance, sometimes Lhermitte sign.
- Hyperreflexia in arms and legs, Hoffmann sign, Babinski, an **inverted brachioradialis reflex** (finger flexion when tapping brachioradialis, indicating C5–C6 level involvement).
- MRI: canal stenosis with cord compression and sometimes T2 signal change in the cord.
- Moderate or severe or progressive myelopathy is generally treated with **decompression** (anterior discectomy/corpectomy and fusion, or posterior laminoplasty or laminectomy and fusion) to halt progression; recovery is better when surgery is earlier.

**Acute UMN weakness is an emergency until proven otherwise**: stroke (time-critical reperfusion), cord compression from tumor, abscess or hematoma. Acute cord compression may present flaccid and areflexic due to spinal shock, so don't be falsely reassured by absent reflexes.

**Spasticity management**: stretching and physiotherapy, orthoses, oral baclofen (GABA-B agonist) or tizanidine (alpha-2 agonist), focal botulinum toxin injections for specific muscles, **intrathecal baclofen pumps** for severe generalized spasticity (abrupt withdrawal is dangerous), and **selective dorsal rhizotomy** in selected children with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.

**Pitfall**: some spasticity helps patients stand and transfer. Treat the goal (pain, hygiene, function), not the tone number.

keyPoints: UMNs descend from cortex/brainstem (corticospinal, corticobulbar) and control LMNs

Pyramidal weakness pattern: arm extensors and leg flexors weakest
Acute lesions may start flaccid (cerebral/spinal shock) and become spastic over days to weeks
Central facial palsy spares the forehead; brainstem lesions give crossed signs
Cervical spondylotic myelopathy: clumsy hands, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann; treated by surgical decompression

lessons.title: Lower Motor Neuron Signs

levels.kid:
The worker nerve cells in your spinal cord are called lower motor neurons. They have wires that go straight to your muscles.

If these worker wires get hurt, the muscle gets no orders at all. So the muscle goes floppy and weak, like a puppet with cut strings.

Without messages, the muscle starts to shrink. You can sometimes see tiny twitches under the skin, like little worms wiggling. When the doctor taps with the reflex hammer, almost nothing happens.

So: hurt boss wires make muscles stiff. Hurt worker wires make muscles floppy!
levels.hs:
**Lower motor neurons (LMNs)** are the motor neurons in the **ventral horn** of the spinal cord and in brainstem motor nuclei. Their axons travel through **ventral roots**, **plexuses** and **peripheral nerves** directly to muscles. Sherrington called them the **final common pathway**: every movement must go through them.

Signs of LMN damage:
- **Weakness** in the muscles supplied by that neuron, root or nerve
- **Flaccid** (floppy) tone
- **Reduced or absent reflexes**
- **Atrophy**: muscles shrink noticeably within weeks
- **Fasciculations**: small visible twitches of motor units under the skin
- Plantar response normal (toes down) or absent, never Babinski

Compare with UMN signs: UMN = stiff, brisk reflexes, little wasting. LMN = floppy, weak reflexes, wasting and twitches.

Where LMN problems happen:
- **Cell bodies**: polio, spinal muscular atrophy, ALS
- **Roots**: a slipped disc pinching a nerve root
- **Peripheral nerves**: injuries, diabetic neuropathy, **Guillain-Barré syndrome**

A classic example is **Bell's palsy**: the facial nerve (an LMN) is affected, so the **entire** half of the face droops, including the forehead.
levels.college:
**LMNs**: alpha motor neurons in the anterior horn and cranial nerve motor nuclei, with axons in ventral roots, plexuses and nerves. Damage anywhere along this path produces the **LMN syndrome**: weakness in a segmental, root or nerve distribution, hypotonia, hyporeflexia or areflexia, prominent atrophy, fasciculations, and on EMG **fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves** (spontaneous single-fiber activity from denervation, appearing about 2–3 weeks after axonal injury).

**Localization along the LMN pathway:**
- **Anterior horn cell**: pure motor, asymmetric weakness with fasciculations, no sensory loss. Examples: ALS (with UMN signs), spinal muscular atrophy (SMN1 deletion), poliomyelitis and other enteroviruses (acute flaccid myelitis).
- **Root (radiculopathy)**: myotomal weakness, dermatomal pain and sensory loss, reduced corresponding reflex.
- **Plexus**: multiple roots and nerves in one limb (e.g., brachial neuritis).
- **Peripheral nerve**: mononeuropathy (single nerve distribution with sensory loss), polyneuropathy (distal, symmetric, length-dependent), or acute demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy.

**Guillain-Barré syndrome**: often post-infectious (Campylobacter jejuni, among others), rapidly progressive symmetric weakness, areflexia, mild sensory symptoms, possible autonomic instability and respiratory failure. CSF shows high protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation). Treat with IVIG or plasma exchange; steroids are not helpful.

**Not LMN, but cause weakness:**
- **NMJ disease**: fatigable weakness, normal reflexes, no atrophy early.
- **Myopathy**: proximal weakness, reflexes preserved until late, no fasciculations, often raised creatine kinase.

**Peripheral (LMN) facial palsy** affects the whole ipsilateral face including the forehead, unlike central palsy.

**ALS** combines UMN and LMN signs in the same regions, sparing sensation and usually eye movements and sphincters. Riluzole and edaravone are disease-modifying; tofersen targets SOD1-related ALS.
levels.phd:
**Denervation biology.** After axotomy, the distal axon undergoes **Wallerian degeneration** over days, mediated by an active program: loss of the axonal survival factor NMNAT2 activates **SARM1**, an NAD+ hydrolase, triggering axon self-destruction. SARM1 inhibition protects axons in models and is a therapeutic target. Denervated muscle fibers spread AChRs (re-expressing fetal gamma-subunit receptors) across the membrane, becoming supersensitive and generating spontaneous fibrillations.

**Fasciculations** are spontaneous discharges of whole motor units, arising from hyperexcitable distal axons or the cell body. They occur in healthy people (benign fasciculation syndrome) and are pathological in context: in ALS they coexist with weakness, atrophy and EMG denervation. The Awaji criteria treat fasciculation potentials as equivalent to fibrillations in the presence of chronic neurogenic change.

**Reinnervation.** Surviving axons sprout collaterally to adopt orphaned fibers, enlarging motor units: on EMG, motor unit potentials become large, long and polyphasic with reduced recruitment. Collateral sprouting can mask motor neuron loss until a large proportion is gone, explaining why ALS and post-polio syndrome become clinically apparent late. Motor unit number estimation (MUNE, MUNIX) quantifies the loss.

**Selective vulnerability.** In ALS, fast fatigable motor units degenerate first and slow units last; oculomotor neurons and Onuf's nucleus (sphincter motor neurons) are relatively spared. Proposed reasons include differences in calcium buffering, AMPA receptor GluA2 editing, ER stress susceptibility, expression of protective factors such as IGF-2 in resistant oculomotor neurons, and MMP-9 expression in vulnerable fast motor neurons.

**Genetic therapies.** Spinal muscular atrophy shows proof-of-concept for LMN disease: nusinersen (antisense oligonucleotide promoting SMN2 exon 7 inclusion), risdiplam (oral splicing modifier) and onasemnogene abeparvovec (AAV9 SMN1 gene replacement) transformed survival, especially with presymptomatic treatment after newborn screening. In ALS, tofersen lowers SOD1 protein and neurofilament light chain, a biomarker of axonal injury.
levels.expert:
**Peripheral nerve injury is a neurosurgical problem.** Classify the injury because it predicts recovery:
- **Seddon**: neurapraxia (conduction block, myelin injury, recovers in weeks), axonotmesis (axon disrupted, connective tissue intact, regenerates), neurotmesis (nerve transected, needs repair).
- **Sunderland** grades I–V subdivide these by connective tissue layers.

**Timing rules:**
- Sharp, clean laceration with deficit: early primary repair (within days).
- Blunt or stretch injury in continuity: observe and repeat EMG at about 3 months; explore if no clinical or electrical recovery.
- Axons regenerate at roughly 1 mm per day (about an inch a month). Muscle end plates degrade if not reinnervated within roughly 12–18 months, so a target far from the injury may never recover with direct repair. **Nerve transfers** (e.g., Oberlin transfer of an ulnar fascicle to biceps after upper brachial plexus injury) bring a donor axon close to the target.

**EMG/NCS timing**: fibrillations take 2–3 weeks to appear; a study done too early can look falsely reassuring. In neurapraxia, conduction is blocked across the lesion but normal distally.

**Patterns to recognize:**
- **Foot drop**: L5 radiculopathy vs common fibular neuropathy vs sciatic or lumbosacral plexus injury; test inversion and hip abduction.
- **Wrist drop**: radial nerve at the spiral groove (Saturday night palsy) spares triceps.
- **Claw hand and intrinsic wasting**: ulnar neuropathy, C8–T1 radiculopathy, or ALS (split hand: thenar and first dorsal interosseous wasted more than hypothenar).
- **Cauda equina syndrome**: LMN signs in both legs, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention; an emergency for **surgical decompression**.

**Guillain-Barré**: track vital capacity, swallowing and autonomic instability; admit to monitored care; IVIG or plasma exchange.

**Pitfall**: in ALS, don't attribute LMN signs to a compressive cervical lesion just because the MRI shows spondylosis; tongue fasciculations or widespread denervation on EMG point beyond the neck, and unneeded surgery helps no one.

keyPoints: LMNs: anterior horn/brainstem motor neurons and their axons in roots, plexuses and nerves (final common pathway)
LMN signs: weakness, flaccidity, hypo/areflexia, early atrophy, fasciculations; fibrillations on EMG after 2–3 weeks
Peripheral facial palsy (e.g., Bell's) affects the whole half-face including the forehead
Guillain-Barré: ascending weakness, areflexia, high CSF protein with normal cells; IVIG or plasma exchange
ALS = UMN + LMN signs with spared sensation; SMA = SMN1 loss, treated with splicing modifiers or gene therapy
Seddon: neurapraxia, axonotmesis, neurotmesis; axons regrow about 1 mm/day

lessons.title: Tone, Reflexes & Babinski

levels.kid:
When the doctor taps just below your knee with a rubber hammer, your leg kicks by itself. You didn't even decide to! That is a reflex.

The tap stretches your muscle a tiny bit. A sensor in the muscle sends a quick message to your spinal cord, and the spinal cord sends a message right back: "Kick!" Your brain isn't even in charge.

Doctors also check how floppy or stiff your arm feels when they move it. That's called tone.

And they scratch the bottom of your foot. Grown-ups' toes curl down. Babies' big toes go up, and that's normal for babies!
levels.hs:
**Reflexes** are automatic responses that use a loop called a **reflex arc**.

The **knee jerk** (patellar reflex):
1. The tap stretches the quadriceps tendon and muscle.
2. **Muscle spindles** detect the stretch.
3. A sensory neuron carries the signal into the spinal cord.
4. It connects **directly** to a motor neuron (a **monosynaptic** reflex).
5. The motor neuron makes the quadriceps contract, and the leg kicks.
At the same time, an interneuron relaxes the hamstrings (**reciprocal inhibition**).

Doctors test reflexes at different spinal levels: biceps (C5–C6), triceps (C7), knee (L4), ankle (S1). They grade them from 0 (absent) to 4+ (very brisk with clonus); 2+ is normal.

**Tone** is the resistance felt when a doctor moves a relaxed limb.
- **Spasticity**: stiff, worse with fast movement (UMN damage)
- **Rigidity**: stiff at any speed, sometimes cogwheel-like (Parkinson disease)
- **Hypotonia**: floppy (LMN damage or cerebellar disease)

**Babinski sign**: stroke the outer sole from heel to toes. Adults' toes curl down (normal). If the big toe goes **up** and toes fan out, it suggests damage to the corticospinal tract. Babies normally have an upgoing toe until about age 1–2, because their corticospinal tract is still maturing.
levels.college:
**Stretch (myotatic) reflex**: muscle spindle group Ia afferents synapse monosynaptically on alpha motor neurons of the same (homonymous) muscle and synergists; collaterals excite **Ia inhibitory interneurons** to the antagonist (reciprocal inhibition). **Gamma motor neurons** innervate intrafusal fibers to keep spindles taut during contraction (**alpha-gamma coactivation**). Golgi tendon organs (Ib) produce **autogenic inhibition** via inhibitory interneurons, limiting excessive tension.

**Reflex levels**: biceps C5–C6, brachioradialis C6 (C5–C6), triceps C7, patellar L4 (L3–L4), Achilles S1. **Grading (NINDS)**: 0 absent, 1+ reduced, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ very brisk with clonus. Asymmetry matters more than absolute grade. **Jendrassik maneuver** (clenching hands or teeth) reinforces a hard-to-elicit reflex.

**Tone abnormalities**:
- **Spasticity**: velocity-dependent, clasp-knife (resistance then sudden release), predominant in antigravity muscles; UMN.
- **Rigidity**: velocity-independent, lead-pipe or cogwheel (tremor superimposed); basal ganglia (parkinsonism).
- **Paratonia (gegenhalten)**: involuntary resistance that varies with examiner force; frontal lobe or diffuse disease.
- **Hypotonia**: LMN lesions, cerebellar lesions (with pendular reflexes), acute shock states.

**Babinski sign (extensor plantar response)**: stroking the lateral sole produces great toe dorsiflexion (extensor hallucis longus) with or without fanning. Indicates corticospinal dysfunction. Alternatives: **Chaddock** (lateral foot), **Oppenheim** (down the shin). Normal in infants.

**Hoffmann sign**: flicking the distal phalanx of the middle finger causes thumb and index flexion; suggests UMN involvement, especially cervical myelopathy.

**Clonus**: repetitive rhythmic contractions after sudden stretch; a few beats can be normal, sustained clonus is pathological.

**Superficial reflexes** (abdominal, cremasteric) are polysynaptic and lost in UMN lesions. **Primitive reflexes** (grasp, snout) re-emerge in frontal disease.
levels.phd:
**What the tendon tap really tests.** The "monosynaptic" reflex is a simplification: the afferent volley is dispersed in time and oligosynaptic pathways contribute to the later part of the response. The **H-reflex** (Hoffmann reflex), elicited electrically by stimulating Ia afferents in the tibial nerve while recording soleus, bypasses the spindle and isolates the spinal component. Comparing H-reflex and tendon reflex separates spinal excitability from fusimotor drive. The H/M ratio rises in spasticity, while H-reflex rate-dependent depression (post-activation depression) is reduced, a marker of altered Ia synaptic function after UMN lesions.

**Fusimotor control.** Gamma motor neurons are independently controllable: static gamma drive biases length sensitivity, dynamic gamma drive increases velocity sensitivity. Microneurography in humans shows fusimotor drive is mostly coactivated with alpha drive and does not set spindle sensitivity independently at rest, which argues against the old "gamma spasticity" model.

**Clonus mechanism.** Clonus arises from a self-sustaining oscillation: stretch evokes a reflex contraction; relaxation re-stretches the muscle, re-triggering the reflex. The frequency (often 5–8 per second at the ankle) depends on reflex loop delay and muscle mechanics, not on a central oscillator, although central rhythm generators may contribute.

**Babinski mechanism.** The plantar response belongs to the nociceptive flexion reflex of the leg. In normal adults, corticospinal input selectively suppresses the toe-extensor component, so the toe flexes. With corticospinal dysfunction, extensor hallucis longus is recruited as part of the limb's shortening (withdrawal) synergy, often with hip and knee flexion. The sign can appear transiently in deep sleep, postictally, after general anesthesia, in hypoglycemia and in deep coma, all states of reduced corticospinal function.

**Interrater reliability** is mediocre for reflex grading and only moderate for the Babinski sign; asymmetric findings and convergent signs carry the diagnostic weight. Clinical neurologists weigh the whole pattern rather than any single sign.
levels.expert:
**Making reflexes decisive.**
- Position the limb relaxed and symmetric; strike briskly; compare side to side immediately.
- Use **Jendrassik reinforcement** before calling a reflex absent.
- Look for **spread** (tapping the biceps also contracts finger flexors), **crossed adductor** responses, and a **pathologically brisk jaw jerk**: a brisk jaw jerk places the lesion above the foramen magnum, while a normal jaw jerk with brisk limb reflexes suggests a cervical cord process.

**Localization with reflex patterns:**
- Brisk below a level and absent at the level: cord or root compression at that level (e.g., inverted brachioradialis at C5–C6).
- Absent ankle jerks with upgoing toes: combined UMN and LMN or neuropathy plus myelopathy (B12 deficiency, Friedreich ataxia, ALS, conus lesions).
- Generalized symmetric 3+ reflexes without other signs may be normal in anxious young people or hyperthyroidism; asymmetric reflexes or sustained clonus are never normal.

**Babinski pitfalls**: stroke the lateral sole firmly but not painfully; withdrawal of the whole foot is not a Babinski. Use Chaddock if the patient is ticklish. A silent (absent) plantar response is not informative.

**Tone scoring**: the **Modified Ashworth Scale** (0, 1, 1+, 2, 3, 4) grades resistance; the Tardieu scale compares slow and fast stretch angles to separate spasticity from contracture. These guide botulinum toxin targeting, intrathecal baclofen trials and selective dorsal rhizotomy decisions.

**Rigidity vs spasticity at the bedside**: activating the opposite limb (opening and closing the hand) increases parkinsonian rigidity (Froment maneuver). Rigidity is equal in flexors and extensors throughout range; spasticity favors antigravity muscles and gives a catch.

**In the ICU and trauma bay**: new unilateral hyperreflexia or Babinski in a head-injured patient suggests an evolving mass lesion; bilateral Babinski signs can occur in deep coma of any cause, so interpret them with the whole exam.

**Pitfall**: never document reflexes as "normal" without testing them; cauda equina and cord compression have been missed because reflexes and the plantar response were assumed rather than examined.

keyPoints: Stretch reflex: spindle Ia afferent → monosynaptic excitation of the alpha motor neuron; reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist
Reflex levels: biceps C5–C6, brachioradialis C6, triceps C7, knee L4, ankle S1; grade 0–4+, 2+ normal
Spasticity = velocity-dependent (UMN); rigidity = velocity-independent, lead-pipe/cogwheel (basal ganglia)
Babinski: great toe extends on stroking the lateral sole = corticospinal dysfunction; normal in infants
Hoffmann sign and sustained clonus are UMN signs; superficial reflexes are lost
Jendrassik maneuver reinforces reflexes before calling them absent
